client: Lately, I’ve been feeling completely overwhelmed with sadness after losing my grandmother last month. It’s been really hard to process, and I’m also worried about my mom—she’s struggling with her grief, and I don’t know how to help her. I’m not sure if therapy can really make a difference with something like this; it just feels like something I have to endure.
therapist:
It sounds like you're carrying both your own grief and concern for your mom right now - that's a heavy load to bear. I notice your voice sounds quite flat while describing these painful feelings; would you say you're feeling emotionally exhausted by it all? 

What comes up for you when you think about the idea of not having to just endure this pain alone?
vocal_descriptors: very high pitch, very quiet, moderate-paced speech

client: Yeah, I do feel exhausted. It’s like I’m constantly carrying this weight, and I don’t even know how to share it with anyone. When you say not enduring it alone, I guess I feel skeptical—like, who would even want to help me with this? It feels like my problem to deal with, and I don’t want to burden anyone else.
therapist:
Your voice sounds higher and quieter than usual when you talk about not wanting to burden others - that makes me wonder if there's some fear underneath that skepticism about reaching out. 

It's understandable to feel protective of others, but I'm curious - what would it be like to imagine someone genuinely wanting to support you through this?
vocal_descriptors: very high pitch, soft-spoken, moderate-paced speech

client: I guess I do feel afraid of being a burden... it’s like I don’t want to impose on anyone or make them feel obligated to help me. Imagining someone genuinely wanting to support me feels nice, but it’s hard to believe it could really happen. I keep thinking they’re just being polite or that I’ll end up disappointing them.
therapist:
It sounds like there's a part of you that longs for support but feels hesitant to truly accept it - almost as if you're preparing yourself for disappointment before it even happens. 

Your voice sounds faster and higher than usual as you share this - what's it like to notice that fear of imposition sitting alongside the wish for connection?
vocal_descriptors: very high pitch, soft-spoken, fast speech

client:
That actually makes me feel kind of exposed, like you're seeing something I didn't even realize about myself. I do want connection, but every time I start to reach out, I hear this voice saying "they're just being polite" or "you're bothering them." 

It's frustrating because part of me knows that's probably not true, but the fear feels so real in the moment. Like if I expect rejection, it won't hurt as much when it happens.
therapist:
That protective instinct to brace for rejection makes so much sense - it's like your mind's way of trying to shield you from pain. I notice your voice gets quicker and quieter when you talk about that fear, almost like part of you wants to rush past the vulnerability. 

What would it feel like to slow down just enough to notice when that protective voice shows up, without needing to either obey or fight it right away?
vocal_descriptors: very high pitch, soft-spoken, very rapid speech

client: I guess I do feel myself speeding up when I talk about rejection—it’s like I want to get it out before someone interrupts or dismisses me. But slowing down feels scary because then I’d have to sit with those feelings, and I don’t know if I can handle how raw that might feel. What if I just get stuck in the pain instead of moving past it?
therapist:
It sounds like there's a real tension between wanting to protect yourself by rushing past these feelings, and the fear that if you slow down, you might get overwhelmed by them. Your voice gets very quiet and quick when you describe this - almost like you're trying to tiptoe past something painful.

What do you imagine might happen if you allowed yourself to feel just a little bit of that rawness in a safe space, without the pressure to immediately move past it?
vocal_descriptors: very high pitch, very quiet, very rapid speech

client:
I don't know...when I try to slow down and actually feel things, it's like opening a door I won't be able to close again. Last time I let myself cry about being lonely, I couldn't stop for hours and then felt exhausted for days. 

Part of me thinks it's better to just keep moving forward, even if it means feeling numb. At least then I can still function at work and with friends. If I really let myself feel everything, I'm scared I'll just fall apart completely.
therapist:
It sounds like you've had experiences where emotions felt overwhelming once you let them in, and that's made you wary of opening that door again. I notice your voice gets higher and faster when talking about that fear of falling apart - almost like your body is already bracing against that possibility. 

What would it be like to experiment with opening that door just a crack, rather than all the way? To let in small amounts of feeling at a time, in ways that might feel more manageable?
vocal_descriptors: very high pitch, moderate volume, fast speech

client:
I get what you're saying about small steps, but even that feels risky. Last time I tried to let myself feel just a little sad, it turned into this huge wave of crying that lasted hours. I'm scared that once I start, I won't be able to stop it from taking over. 

It's like... I know logically that emotions aren't dangerous, but my body reacts like they are. My chest gets tight just thinking about trying this.
therapist:
I hear how frightening that experience was for you - it makes complete sense that you'd be cautious after feeling so overwhelmed last time. Your voice gets very high and quick when describing this, like your body is already preparing for danger at just the thought of feeling sad. 

What if we thought about ways to help your body feel safe first, before even approaching those emotions? Like creating some grounding tools you could reach for if things start feeling too intense?
vocal_descriptors: very high pitch, soft-spoken, very rapid speech

client: I guess that makes sense, but when I start feeling sad or anxious, it's like my whole body goes on high alert before I even realize what's happening. I don't know if I'll remember to use grounding tools in the moment - that's the problem. It feels like once that wave hits, I'm just along for the ride until it passes.
therapist:
It sounds like those intense emotions hit you so quickly that it feels impossible to intervene in the moment - almost like being caught in a sudden storm. Your voice sounds higher and faster as you describe this, like your body is already anticipating that helpless feeling. 

What if we practiced some grounding techniques right now, while you're feeling calm, to help build that muscle memory before you actually need it? That way, it might feel more automatic when those waves do come.
vocal_descriptors: very high pitch, loud, fast speech

client: I get what you're saying about practicing when I'm calm, but I don't know if it'll help when I'm actually panicking. Last time I tried breathing exercises during an attack, it just made me more frustrated because I couldn't do it "right." My mind races so fast that any technique feels impossible to remember in the moment.
therapist:
It makes sense that trying to "do it right" during panic would add frustration on top of the distress you're already feeling. I notice your voice gets higher when talking about those failed attempts - it sounds like part of you has already decided these techniques won't work for you. 

What if we thought about this differently - not as something to "get right," but as experiments to discover what might help even a tiny bit when you're struggling? Would that feel more manageable to approach?
vocal_descriptors: very high pitch, moderate volume, moderate-paced speech

client:
I guess calling them experiments does sound less intimidating than trying to "fix" my panic attacks perfectly. But part of me still worries that even small attempts will fail, and then I'll just feel worse about myself. That's happened before when I've tried breathing exercises and they didn't stop the panic. 

I do like the idea of taking the pressure off though. Maybe if I didn't expect immediate results, it wouldn't feel so devastating when something doesn't work right away. But how do I stop feeling like a failure when the techniques don't help in the moment? That's what always trips me up.
therapist:
It sounds like past experiences have built up this fear that techniques won't work, which then makes it even harder to try them without pressure. Your voice softens as you talk about this cycle - I wonder if part of you is already bracing for disappointment before even giving it a chance.

What if we reframed "failure" as valuable information? Each attempt, even if it doesn't provide immediate relief, could teach us something about what might help - or at least what doesn't work for you. How might that perspective shift feel?
vocal_descriptors: very high pitch, soft-spoken, fast speech
